opening.headline: We answer the question of how much permission to grant a coding agent safely through a four-layer authorization structure: rules, modes, hooks, and sandbox.
body: The coding agent can run npm test for a day, clear the build folder, attempt to upload files to an external address, read an .env file, and try a git push. If it were to prompt for every command, the agent would be unable to perform tasks; if all commands were allowed without restriction, deletion and data leakage, along with remote synchronization, could occur simultaneously.

In this class, we examine permissions divided into three layers, centered on the Claude Code documentation. We look at allowance, verification, and denial rules along with their priority levels, permission modes that define scope without approval, hooks that block code execution just before tool calls, and sandboxes that restrict the impact scope of shell commands. Finally, we discuss a case where dangerous commands still pass through despite the presence of hooks, and verify the rationale for implementing multiple layers of protection.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Permission rules, permission modes, hooks, and sandboxes each have their respective roles.
You can analyze the evaluation order and priority of allow, confirm, and deny rules to determine what results will occur.

screens.title: How much should we allow coding agents to be safe?
screens.lead: Review the commands that a coding agent can attempt within a day. The diagram shows the level of risk associated with each command.

visual.alt: A diagram listing five commands attempted by a coding agent and the risk level associated with each command.
labels: Upload a file to an external address using curl
Asked every time → Unable to do the work
All allowed → Delete, leak, reflect in one go
The solution is not one but multiple layers.

paragraphs: Let's suppose a coding agent tried these commands within a single day: running npm test, deleting the build folder with rm -rf build, uploading a file to an external address using curl, reading an .env file, and performing a git push.

If we repeatedly ask humans to approve each of these commands, the agent will hardly perform any tasks. Conversely, if we allow all commands without restriction, deletion, data leakage, and remote modifications could occur simultaneously. Since the risk level varies from command to command, they cannot be treated uniformly under a single standard.

Approval alone is not sufficient to resolve this issue. Rules, modes, hooks, and sandboxes each address the same problem at different layers. Rules define the baseline of behavior, modes set the frequency of validation, hooks block exceptions at the code level, and sandboxes limit the scope of impact.
In this class, we will distinguish each layer one by one, centered on the Claude Code documentation. The same principles apply to other agent products.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If one out of three layers is empty, what happens? In the case study, we verify how another layer prevents the missed command.

screens.outro: First, let's check what permissions your agent has.

screens.title: Preview: Permissions assigned to the agent
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please first mentally review the answer before clicking it.

items.prompt: Do agents know which files they can read and which domains they can connect to?
items.answer: Mostly, it is not precisely known. In the default state, the agent can read files outside the working directory, and it is not immediately obvious which external addresses it can connect to. The first step in checking permissions is to verify what is currently open.

items.prompt: Is a device that blocks dangerous commands based solely on the model's judgment, or is it enforced by code?
items.answer: The model's judgment may be wrong or misleading. Mechanisms designed to block dangerous commands should ideally be enforced through code. The rules, hooks, and sandboxes discussed in this course all operate independently of the model's judgment.

items.prompt: Will the next layer block when one layer is pierced?
items.answer: If defense is only relying on a single layer, the protection fails the moment that layer is compromised. Since the targets to be blocked and vulnerabilities differ from one layer to another, having multiple layers is the principle. This lesson's case analysis directly verifies this concept.

screens.outro: Let's continue with the following check items, addressing them floor by floor on the next screen.

screens.title: Permission Rules: Allow, Confirm, Deny and Priority
screens.lead: The following are permission rules to be written in the settings.json of Claude Code. Please check the right-side explanations for the meaning of each line, symptoms when they mismatch, and evaluation order.

notes.note: Allow rules are in effect. Commands starting with "npm run" or "git commit" execute without approval. * indicates a variable part. If the rules do not match the actual commands used, frequently executed commands will prompt for approval each time.
The ask rule does not automatically approve the command. In dontAsk mode, it denies without displaying a confirmation window. In other modes, it follows the respective approval or review pathway.

This is a deny rule. Commands starting with "aws" and reading from the .env file are blocked. Deny rules are also enforced in bypassPermissions mode. However, the rule matches exactly by character, so commands that differ slightly (e.g., "git -C . push") may not match this rule and thus may not be blocked.

The evaluation order is deny, ask, allow, and the first matching rule determines the outcome. The specificity of rules cannot be altered by changing the order. Even if you add a narrow allow rule such as Bash (aws s3 ls), a broader deny rule like Bash (aws *) will match first and block it. An allow rule cannot create exceptions within a deny rule. A deny rule that specifies only the tool name (e.g., Bash) completely removes that tool from Claude's context. Rules are stored in the configuration file, shared with the team, and verified under /permissions.

screens.outro: If rules define the baseline, the boundaries permissible without approval are determined by the authorization mode.

screens.title: Permission mode: Range that becomes active without approval
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn about the scope of execution allowed without approval in each permission mode and the appropriate use cases.

tabs.label: default (Manual)
tabs.body: Execution occurs without approval for reading only. Actions such as modifying files, executing shell commands, or accessing the network are prompted for confirmation first. It is appropriate when you want to review all actions directly or when performing sensitive operations. The setting value is `default` and it also has the alias `manual` in the CLI.

tabs.label: acceptEdits
tabs.body: Reading and file modification, as well as common file system commands such as mkdir, touch, mv, and cp, are automatically permitted. This is appropriate when refining existing code under direct review. Writing to protected paths and removal of core paths via rm are still pending.

tabs.label: plan and auto
tabs.body: plan is a mode that explores the codebase and establishes plans before modifying code, during which modifications are blocked until the plan is approved. auto employs a separate classification model to review actions on behalf of humans, preventing actions that exceed the requested scope or are triggered by adversarial content, thereby reducing fatigue from prolonged approval processes. Explicit ask rules are still queried even within auto.

tabs.label: dontAsk
tabs.body: Reads files within the working directory and allows only pre-approved tools; all other actions are rejected without inquiry. Suitable for locked CI or scripts without human oversight.

tabs.label: bypassPermissions
tabs.body: Allows all actions. It is recommended to use it only within isolated containers and VMs. Even in this mode, deny rules are enforced, and certain actions (such as tools specified in explicit ask rules or rm deletion on core paths) are not automatically approved. This mode serves as a baseline, upon which additional rules can be layered to explicitly allow or block specific tools.

screens.outro: If rules and modes ask things of people, then a hook is a device that intercepts calls made in code.

screens.title: Hook (PreToolUse) and execution timeline
screens.lead: Follow step by step to see when the hook inserts into the agent's execution and how the setting is read. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: Timeline within the agent loop involving PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, tool execution, and PostToolUse.

steps.title: What is a hook?
steps.body: A hook is a user-defined handler that automatically executes at predefined points in the lifecycle. A shell command, an HTTP endpoint, an MCP tool call, a prompt, or a sub-agent can serve as a hook. It runs at events such as session start, before user prompt transmission, before or after tool calls, and session end.

steps.title: When to run
steps.body: When calling a tool within an agent loop, events occur in the following order: PreToolUse (before execution, cancellable), PermissionRequest (when permission determination is needed), and PostToolUse (after execution). PreToolUse, which occurs before the tool is executed, is appropriate for preventing dangerous calls.

steps.title: Read settings
steps.body:
The following configuration runs a script only for commands starting with "rm" in Bash tool calls.

``json
{"hooks": {"PreToolUse": [{"matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "if": "Bash(rm *)", "command": "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/block-rm.sh"}]}]}}
```

`matcher` determines which tool calls it responds to. If mismatched, the hook will not execute at all, and blocking will not occur. `if` runs the script only when a subcommand matches Bash(rm *). If omitted, the script will execute for all calls matching the matcher.

steps.title: Blocking and forwarding
steps.body: If the script makes a deny decision, the call is not executed, and the reason is passed to Claude, prompting it to explore alternative approaches. If the script does not make a decision, the usual authorization flow continues. The key point is that it is the code enforcing the decision, not the model's judgment. Even if the model is persuaded or makes a mistake, the hook's validation proceeds in the same manner.

steps.title: Organization-level hook
steps.body: In an enterprise environment, inference hooks can be used to send all prompts and tool calls to the organization's server, where they receive an allow or deny decision before proceeding. This approach enforces organizational policies from a single point, beyond individual settings.

screens.outro: The final layer, the sandbox, and we'll examine the permission model of other products.

screens.title: Authorization model different from sandbox
screens.lead: Select an item to expand and verify the scope and limitations of the sandbox, as well as the permission structure of other products.

items.title: Claude Code Bash Sandbox
items.body: Executes shell commands within boundaries enforced by the operating system. Writing is restricted to the working directory and temporary directory, among others. Network access is not allowed directly but must go through the user's computer's proxy, and the initial list of allowed domains is empty. Reading is generally permitted for most device contents, including credential files such as ~/.ssh, so a read-exclusion scope should be configured if necessary. The sandbox is disabled by default and can be enabled by setting it to /sandbox.

items.title: What is not covered by the sandbox
items.body: The sandbox only restricts shell commands. File reading, editing, and writing tools, as well as web tools, run outside the sandbox and are controlled by permission rules. Other processes such as hooks or the local MCP server are executed with full access privileges. Therefore, simply enabling the sandbox does not isolate all tools; the remaining components must be separately blocked using rules and hooks.

items.title: Sandbox mode
items.body: In auto-allow mode, commands executed within the sandbox are run without being prompted. The operating system enforces the boundary. In regular permissions mode, general permission checks are maintained even within the sandbox. Either way, deny rules are applied unchanged.

items.title: OpenAI Sandbox Agents
items.body: OpenAI also recommends the same separation. A harness manages agent loops, model calls, tool routing, approval, tracing, and recovery within a trusted zone, while commands and file operations are executed in an isolated sandbox compute environment with limited credentials and mounted volumes. Authentication, billing, audit logs, and human review are kept outside the container.

items.title: App permissions and delegation access
items.body: ChatGPT's app permissions always include stages such as "prompt," "read access," and "low-risk access," and workspace policies can override these. The Microsoft ID platform distinguishes between delegated access on behalf of users and app-specific access that uses only the app's own identity, requesting permissions only when necessary. Although the product may differ, the principle that it opens only the required features and that higher-level policies take precedence remains the same.

screens.outro: Having viewed all three cases, I will now explain a hazardous command that has already been executed, using it as a case study.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Reason Why a Dangerous Instruction Passed Even Though a Hook Was Attached
screens.lead: The instructor analyzes the script code to explain why the block-rm.sh hook failed to prevent the agent from executing rm -fr ./build. Follow along and check where the discrepancy occurs by reading the right-side explanation.

data.code:
COMMAND=$(jq -r '.tool_input.command')

if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -q 'rm -rf'; then
  jq -n '{hookSpecificOutput: {
    hookEventName: "PreToolUse",
    permissionDecision: "deny",
    permissionDecisionReason: "Destructive command blocked by hook"}}'
else
  exit 0
fi

notes.note: The hook receives JSON via standard input. This line extracts tool_input.command, i.e., the command string the agent intends to execute. In this scenario, the hook actually ran because the matcher matched Bash and the if condition matched "rm *". Thus, the issue is not that the hook did not run.

grep -q 'rm -rf' searches for the literal substring 'rm -rf'. The command executed by the agent was 'rm -fr ./build', and since the flag order differs, it does not match the substring. The meaning is the same deletion command, but the check condition was incorrectly specified.

Output when a match is found. If permissionDecision is set to deny along with a reason, the call is blocked and the reason is passed to Claude. If it does not enter this quarter, blocking will not occur.

When a mismatch occurs, it terminates with exit code 0. Exit code 0 means neither allowed nor denied—it signifies no decision. Thus, the normal authorization flow continues. Approval requests are displayed or executed as per the mode and rules. The symptom is that a hook is present but blocking does not occur.

screens.outro: Having identified the script's vulnerabilities, I'll now organize the approach to fix them and strengthen them with additional safeguards.

screens.title: Permissions are stacked: three layers of configuration and priority analysis
screens.lead: The table below summarizes, based on the example, what each of the four layers blocks, where gaps might occur, and how one layer supports the next. Please read it row by row, linking each point to the example.

data.caption: Three roles, weaknesses, mitigation methods
rows: Defines the basic policy of actions using allow, ask, and deny. The evaluation order is deny, ask, allow, and the first matching rule determines the outcome.
If commands are written differently, rules and characters will not match, leading to missed matches. Commands not defined in the rules cannot be handled.
The hook expresses flexibility in checking code, and the sandbox limits the scope of commands that can reach it.
Sets the threshold for confirmation frequency without approval
Mode alone cannot distinguish individual commands. bypassPermissions allows all.
Deny rules block in all modes. Bypass is only used in isolated environments.
Blocks or allows specific calls via code just before tool invocation
Conditions that are missed in the check are passed over without decision. The rm -fr case is an example of this.
Broaden the inspection conditions and concurrently enforce deny rules to effectively block unwanted access. The sandbox restricts write scope.
The write scope and network of shell commands are restricted at the operating system level.
Only shell commands are sandboxed. File tools, MCP server, and hooks run outside the sandbox.
The File Tools and MCP are separately controlled through permission rules and hooks.
data.notes: The key points of priority analysis are three. First, deny takes precedence over allow, so the boundary is established first with deny, and allow applies only outside of that boundary. Second, even in bypassPermissions, deny still blocks access, so the boundary remains defined by deny even in isolated environments. Third, sandboxing applies only to the shell, so file tools and MCP are blocked through rules and hooks. The two inspection questions are: if one layer is empty, does the next layer still provide protection? And is the system solely dependent on human approval?

screens.outro: We will summarize the entire authorization structure, including the conclusion of the case.

screens.title: Authority structure in one page
screens.lead: We summarize and organize the previous content into lessons learned from four roles and examples.

paragraphs: Permission rules are evaluated in the order of deny, ask, allow, and the first matching rule determines the outcome. The deny line is drawn first, and allow is applied outside of that line. The permission boundary defines the scope within which approval is not required, and rules are superimposed upon this boundary.

Hook determines, via code, whether a tool call is blocked or allowed right before the tool call. A key advantage is that it operates in the same manner regardless of the model's judgment. However, if the script terminates without a decision, the normal permission flow continues, so it is necessary to verify that no expressions might miss the intended check conditions.

A sandbox defines the boundary between shell commands and files/networks at the operating system level. However, it does not cover file utilities, MCP servers, or hooks outside the shell, so rules and hooks are required together.

Going back to the initial question, it is not sufficient to define limits for coding agents at a single point. A safer approach is to stack multiple layers such that even if one layer is bypassed, the next layer mitigates the damage, without relying solely on human approval. In the example case, the rm -fr command would have caused less damage if there had been a deny rule or write restrictions enforced by a sandbox.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Permissions are layered. Rules define the baseline, modes determine the check frequency, hooks block code, and sandboxes restrict the scope of impact.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: The configuration includes a broad deny rule for Bash (aws *) and a narrow allow rule for Bash (aws s3 ls). What happens when aws s3 ls is executed?
options: More specific allow takes precedence and thus execution occurs without approval.
Since the rules conflict, the rule that is specified later applies.
Changes to ask result in confirmation being requested from people each time.
deny is evaluated first and is dropped
checks.explain: The evaluation order is deny, ask, allow, and the result is determined by the first matching rule. Specificity cannot change the order, and allow cannot create an exception within deny.

wrong.0: Even if the rules are more specific, they cannot precede deny.
wrong.1: The order of application is deny, ask, allow, not based on the time of writing.
wrong.2: A matching deny determines the outcome, so there is no need to proceed to the verification step.

checks.intro: Pair up the three roles. The result is not recorded.
checks.q: Review the four layers of permissions and pair them with their respective roles.
right: The write scope and network of shell commands are restricted at the operating system level.
Blocks a specific call via code just before tool execution.
Defines the basic principles for action through allow, ask, deny.
Sets the threshold for confirmation frequency without approval
checks.explain: Rules are baseline, modes are check frequencies, hooks are exception blocking at the code level, and sandboxes limit the scope of impact. Each layer prevents the same issue at a different level.

checks.intro: Problem reading the hook script. Results are not recorded.
checks.q:
The hook script looks like this. What happens when the agent runs rm -fr ./build?  
if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -q 'rm -rf'; then (deny output) else exit 0 fi
options: rm -fr deletes a directory, so the hook denies it.
'rm -rf' does not match exactly, ends without decision, and the usual permission flow continues.
The session is terminated entirely due to a script error.
exit 0 means allow, so it executes without applying any rules.
checks.explain: grep looks for literal fragments, so rm -fr does not match. The exit 0 in else indicates undecided, and thus the usual permission flow based on mode and rules continues.

wrong.0: The hook blocks only when the script outputs deny. Even if the meaning is similar, it will not be blocked if it does not match the check condition.
wrong.2: Since there was no decision, the session is not terminated.
wrong.3: exit 0 is not allowed; it is undefined. deny rules are applied as usual.

glossary.def: This setting defines allow, ask, and deny for tools and command patterns. Rules are evaluated in the order of deny, ask, allow, and the first matching rule determines the result.
This is the baseline that defines the scope of actions executed without approval. Options include: default, acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissions.
A handler that executes just before a tool call is performed. It can block or allow the call via code.
This is the boundary that limits the scope of files and networks accessible via shell commands at the operating system level.
This is a mode that allows all actions. It is recommended to use this mode only in isolated containers and VMs, and deny rules still apply in this mode.
In hook configuration, the matcher selects which tool call it should respond to, and the if statement narrows script execution to only those commands that meet specific conditions.

misconceptions.myth: Specific allow rules take precedence over broad deny rules.
misconceptions.fact: The evaluation order is deny, ask, allow, and the first matching rule takes effect. Allow cannot create an exception within deny.

misconceptions.myth: When the sandbox is enabled, all agent tools are isolated.
misconceptions.fact: Sandbox applies only to shell commands. File tools, MCP server, and hooks run outside the sandbox and must be controlled separately using rules and hooks.
Deny rules still apply in this mode. Even so, use this mode only in isolated environments.

misconceptions.myth: Once a hook is attached, all dangerous commands are blocked.
misconceptions.fact: If a script terminates without a decision, the usual authorization flow continues. Expressions where check conditions are overlooked must be addressed by deny rules and sandboxing.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Permissions are stacked. Rules, hooks, sandboxes form layers, and modes define the baseline.
Rules are evaluated in the order of deny, ask, allow, and the first matching rule takes effect.
Hook blocks code before tool invocation and does not rely on the model's judgment.
The sandbox limits the file and network scope of shell commands, and file tools and MCP are separately controlled by rules and hooks.
